# MC 501 Assignments

**Every assignment in this course, grouped by phase, with what it asks for and when it is due.**

Each assignment shows a short description. Open the section under it for what to submit and the printable rubric, which lists what to include, how long, and what earns full credit.

::: {.callout-note}
## How to turn work in

**Submit everything in Blackboard**, under the assignment for that week. Keep your work in your course workspace and commit it to GitHub as usual for the backup and the history, but **committing is not submitting**: grading happens from the Blackboard submission. Get the AURA Lab R Companion from its [Marketplace listing](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=aura-lab-siue.r-companion). Two assignments also ask you to paste a GitHub link into the submission; the link goes in the submission, it does not replace it.

Everything is due at **11:59 PM** on the **Monday** listed. The one exception is the White Paper and poster, due Friday, December 18. You are welcome to submit any assignment early. Attempts are unlimited, so an early submission can still be revised right up to the deadline.

Submissions are **unlimited**. If you upload the wrong file, or want to revise before the deadline, submit again.

**AI-use log:** where an assignment asks for it, the AURA Lab R Companion's output (its setup check, its error explanations, and any code its menus write) is not AI use and is not logged; Copilot is, including any answer Copilot gives using the Companion's tools.
:::


## Every assignment is a part of the paper

Almost nothing here is submitted and then finished. Each assignment builds a component the next one
consumes, and the White Paper is those components assembled and argued.

## Phase III: The Builder {#phase-iii-the-builder}

*Operationalization.* Turn concepts into an instrument a stranger could apply. [Phase page](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/modules/03_builder/?edition=mc501)

### CITI Ethics Certification {#citi-ethics-certification}

**25 points. Due Monday, September 28, 11:59 PM.** *(Week 5)*

Complete the CITI Program's Social and Behavioral Research training, and draft the determination you would actually file.

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>Full requirements</summary>

**What you submit:** two files. The CITI completion certificate as a PDF, and your non-human-subjects determination draft.

**Requirements**

1. The course completed is **Social and Behavioral Research**, the student version, not Responsible Conduct of Research.
2. The institution reads **Southern Illinois University Edwardsville**, your name matches your enrolled name, and the certificate carries its verification ID.
3. **The determination draft**, 300 to 400 words, stating: what your data is, where it came from, whether the people in it are identifiable, why the project does or does not meet the federal definition of human-subjects research, and which exemption or determination category you would claim.
4. The draft names **one fact that would change the answer**. A public corpus that became identifiable through a join is the obvious case, and it is the one your own project runs closest to.

**How it is graded.** Certificate 10, determination 10, the changed-answer paragraph 5.

**Where it comes from.** Week 3 and Chapter 3. **What it feeds:** the methods section of your White Paper, which has to state the determination rather than assume it.

**How this loses points.** Concluding "not human subjects" without naming the definition you applied. The determination is an argument from a rule, not a verdict, and a reviewer will ask which rule.

</details>

### Annotated Manuscripts, three articles {#annotated-manuscripts-three-articles}

**25 points. Due Monday, September 28, 11:59 PM.** *(Week 5)*

Annotate three peer-reviewed articles, then write the paragraph that makes them one body of work rather than three summaries.

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>Full requirements</summary>

**Worked example:** [Annotated manuscript example (PDF)](resources/annotation-example.pdf).

**What you submit:** the three annotated PDFs, plus one document holding the per-article notes and the synthesis.

**Requirements**

1. All three are **peer reviewed** and report original research.
2. For **each** article: the gap the authors claim, the theoretical framework or its absence, the method with unit and sample, the finding in one sentence with its **effect size and n** where reported, and the limitation the authors admit.
3. **A synthesis paragraph**, 200 to 300 words, that names what the three converge on, where they disagree or qualify each other, and the limitation they share.
4. The synthesis **leads with the claim and carries its citations at the end**, in the form (Lastname, YEAR). A chain of author-led sentences is an annotated bibliography, not a synthesis.
5. **One sentence naming the gap** the three leave open, and what your study would do about it.
6. **APA 7 references** for all three.

**How it is graded.** Per-article notes 12, four points each. Synthesis 8. The gap sentence 3. References and the peer-reviewed requirement 2.

**Where it comes from.** Week 4 and Chapter 4. **What it feeds:** the Research Proposal two weeks later, whose introduction is this synthesis with a study attached.

**How this loses points.** Three good summaries and a weak synthesis is the failure this assignment is designed to expose, and it is worth 8 of 25. Picking three articles that agree with each other is the other: convergence with nothing to qualify it gives you nothing to argue with.

</details>

### Topic Selection and Research Questions {#topic-selection-and-research-questions}

**25 points. Due Monday, October 5, 11:59 PM.** *(Week 6)*

Commit to a topic and write the questions your study will answer.

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>Full requirements</summary>

**What you submit:** one document, roughly one page.

**Requirements**

1. **A topic statement** of two to three sentences naming the phenomenon, the population and the context.
2. **One to three research questions**, numbered, each written as a question.
3. **Hypotheses where you have a directional prediction**, labeled H1, H2, each a stated relationship between two variables, each with **one sentence of theoretical justification** for the direction. A prediction with no reason behind it is a guess.
4. **A variable preview**: for each question, the construct, what you would measure, the unit of analysis and the expected level of measurement.
5. **A justification**, 100 to 150 words, of why the answer matters, written for a reader in your field rather than for me.
6. **The five-criteria check** for criteria 1 through 4, one line per criterion per question. Criterion 5 is what your justification above already answers, so do not write it twice.

**How it is graded.** Topic 3, questions 5, hypotheses with justification 5, variable preview 5, why it matters 4, five-criteria check 3.


**Where it comes from.** Weeks 5 and 6, Chapters 5 and 6. **What it feeds:** the Research Proposal, which is these questions with a method and a sampling plan attached.

**How this loses points.** A directional hypothesis with no theory behind it costs the justification points even when the direction turns out right. Submitting a subject rather than a question is the other common one.

**The five criteria, in full**

**Run every question past these before you submit it:**

1. **Specific.** Name the platform, specify the outcome, bound the population. "How does
   social media influence politics?" leaves all three undefined.
2. **Measurable.** Some concepts resist operationalization. "Do authentic streamers build
   better communities?" cannot be studied until *authentic* and *better* become something
   you can record.
3. **Answerable within your constraints.** Decades of data or hundreds of interviews is
   not a semester project.
4. **Not already answered.** Your literature review tells you whether the question is
   genuinely open.
5. **It matters.** A question can be answerable and still be trivia.

Two of these you can check yourself. **Not already answered** and **it matters** are
judgments you make from your reading, and the check asks you to state the judgment and
the evidence behind it.

</details>

### Research Proposal, sentence outline {#research-proposal-sentence-outline}

**75 points. Due Monday, October 12, 11:59 PM.** *(Week 7)*

A structured sentence outline that could serve as the front half of a conference paper.

The [Research Proposal template](mc501-research-proposal-template.qmd) goes through each section with its points, the checks that cost points on Topic Selection, and a weaker and a stronger example. The template's section-by-section points are the rubric.

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>Full requirements</summary>

**What you submit:** one document, 1,200 to 1,800 words, in outline form. Every point is a full sentence carrying a claim, never a topic label. "Parasocial interaction and chat" is a label; "Viewers of smaller channels report stronger parasocial bonds, which should leave a visible trace in how they address the streamer" is a point.

**Worked example:** [Research Proposal worked example (PDF)](resources/examples/MC501-example-research-proposal.pdf). A finished submission, so you can see the form before you write yours.

**Requirements**

1. **Framing**, three to five points: the phenomenon, why it matters now, and what is at stake in getting the answer wrong.
2. **Theoretical positioning**, four to six points naming the lens, what it predicts, and what a competing lens would predict instead. The competing lens is not optional; a framework with no rival is a decoration.
3. **The literature**, six to ten points, organized by theme rather than by author, carrying the convergence, the nuance and the shared limitation. This is your synthesis paragraph expanded.
4. **The gap**, two to three points, resting on that shared limitation.
5. **Research questions or hypotheses**, stated formally, each traceable to a point in the theory section.
6. **The proposed design**, eight to twelve points: unit of analysis, population and frame, sampling method, measurement, the reliability protocol you intend, and the analysis you plan before you see the data.
7. **Contribution**, two to three points, written for your field rather than for this course.
8. **References** in APA 7 for everything cited.

**How it is graded.** Framing 8, theory 15, literature 15, gap 8, questions 10, design 15, contribution 4.

**Where it comes from.** Weeks 5 and 6, Chapters 5 and 6. **What it feeds:** the front half of the White Paper, and the analysis plan you commit to before running anything.

**How this loses points.** Topic labels instead of sentences is the failure this assignment is named for. The second is a design section that names no analysis, which quietly defers every hard decision until after you have seen the data, which is exactly what this term has been arguing against.

</details>

### Extended Codebook and Reliability Protocol {#extended-codebook-and-reliability-protocol}

**75 points. Due Monday, November 2, 11:59 PM.** *(Week 10)*

Build the instrument, then write the protocol that says how you will know it stayed consistent.

**Your coding sheet.** The codebook and the coding sheet work together: the codebook is the document that says what each variable means and which values it can take, and the coding sheet is the spreadsheet you actually code in. Start your coding sheet now so it is ready for the pilot. It has one row for each item you will code (a message, a post, an article) and one column for each variable, named exactly as the variable is named in your codebook. Keep an `id` column so every code can be matched back to its item, and a `coder_notes` column for anything you were unsure about. Download the [coding sheet template (CSV)](resources/templates/coding-sheet-template.csv), rename the `variable_` columns to your own variables (add or delete columns until there is one per variable), and save it in your workspace as `data/coding-sheet.csv`. For the reliability check you code each pilot item twice, so the pilot version adds a second column for each variable (for example `tone_p1` and `tone_p2`), as in the Sampling Plan and Pilot worked example's coded data. The coding sheet is not graded with this assignment; you fill it in for the Sampling Plan and Pilot. For a finished one, open `vr-sample.csv` in [the VR codebook](examples/vr-codebook/mc501-vr-codebook-walkthrough.html).

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>What to submit, and the rubric</summary>

**What you submit:** the codebook and the reliability protocol, as one document with two headed parts, uploaded to Blackboard under Extended Codebook and Reliability Protocol.

**Length:** The codebook 1,200 to 2,000 words, counting its variable and example tables, and the reliability protocol 500 to 900 words. Word counts cover your own writing, not the title, headings, tables, references, figure captions, code, or output, and writing more than the range never costs points.

**Part of the White Paper:** the codebook and the reliability protocol are a draft of the Methods section's measures and reliability plan.

**AI-use log:** submit the [AI-use log (.docx)](resources/AI-use-log.docx) with this assignment, with an entry for each time an AI tool shaped it, or with the no-AI box checked.

**Rubric:** [Extended Codebook and Reliability Protocol rubric (PDF)](resources/rubrics/MC501-rubric-extended-codebook-and-reliability-protocol.pdf). It lists the five parts of the codebook, the five parts of the protocol, and the points for each.

**Starter:** [09-coding-the-codebook.qmd](starters/09-coding-the-codebook.qmd), the Week 9 starter file for coding your codebook in R.

**Worked example:** [Extended Codebook and Reliability Protocol worked example (PDF)](resources/examples/MC501-example-extended-codebook-and-reliability-protocol.pdf). A finished submission, so you can see the form before you write yours.

**Second example:** [the VR codebook](examples/vr-codebook/mc501-vr-codebook-walkthrough.html), a real published study with its downloads.

**Template:** [Extended Codebook and Reliability Protocol template (Quarto .qmd)](resources/templates/MC501-codebook-template.qmd) or [the same template (Word .docx)](resources/templates/MC501-codebook-template.docx). Use it directly as your `codebook/codebook.qmd` or as inspiration for your own layout.

</details>

### Sampling Plan and Pilot, 20 to 30 items {#sampling-plan-and-pilot-20-to-30-items}

**75 points. Due Monday, November 9, 11:59 PM.** *(Week 11)*

Design your sampling strategy (search terms, date range, method) and pilot test your codebook on **20 to 30 items**, a large enough subset to compute a meaningful reliability statistic. Document edge cases, coding decisions, the alpha you obtained, and any revisions the pilot forced.

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>What to submit, and the rubric</summary>

**What you submit:** the plan and the pilot as one document, plus your coded pilot data and the code that computed the reliability figure, uploaded to Blackboard under Sampling Plan and Pilot, 20 to 30 items. Optional: the R Companion's **Reliability grid** takes your pass 1 and pass 2 codes, saves them as a CSV, and writes the `v2v::reliability()` call into your script; that call counts as the code that computed the figure. To code the pilot items in VS Code instead of a spreadsheet, **AURA: Open the data viewer** opens your CSV in a grid where you add your coding columns and code each row; your codes save to `data/derived/`, the original file is never changed, and **Insert rebuild code** writes the lines that join the codes back on. Excel and Google Sheets still work.

**Length:** 700 to 1,200 words across the plan and the pilot write-up, plus 20 to 30 coded items. Word counts cover your own writing, not the title, headings, tables, references, figure captions, code, or output, and writing more than the range never costs points.

**Part of the White Paper:** a draft of the Methods section's sampling plan and reliability report.

**AI-use log:** submit the [AI-use log (.docx)](resources/AI-use-log.docx) with this assignment, with an entry for each time an AI tool shaped it, or with the no-AI box checked.

**Rubric:** [Sampling Plan and Pilot rubric (PDF)](resources/rubrics/MC501-rubric-sampling-plan-and-pilot.pdf). It lists each part of the plan and the pilot with its points, and carries the table for sizing your corpus.

**Worked example:** [Sampling Plan and Pilot worked example (PDF)](resources/examples/MC501-example-sampling-plan-and-pilot.pdf), with its [coded pilot data (CSV)](resources/examples/MC501-sampling-pilot/MC501-pilot-codes.csv) and [stability script (R)](resources/examples/MC501-sampling-pilot/02-pilot-stability.R). A finished submission, so you can see the form before you write yours.

**How-to:** the [Draw your coding sample](guides/mc501/06-draw-your-coding-sample.md) and [Reliability grid](guides/mc501/07-reliability-grid.md) step-by-step guides.

</details>

### Data Wrangling in R {#data-wrangling-in-r}

**50 points. Due Monday, November 16, 11:59 PM.** *(Week 12)*

Build the analysis-ready table from the raw one, in code that runs start to finish.

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>What to submit, and the rubric</summary>

**What you submit:** the filled worksheet and the HTML it renders to, your coded `data/coding-form.csv`, and the exported dataset, saved as `twitch_analysis.RDS` because Describing Data and Inferencing Data both read that file, uploaded to Blackboard under Data Wrangling in R. The worksheet is part 1 of one Twitch job in three worksheets: the code that is not the point is written for you, the core steps are blanks you fill, and the thirty messages you hand-code in its Part 0 are tested in Inferencing Data. Where an R Companion menu writes a step, the worksheet names it, and what the menu writes counts as your code. Export to RDS, not CSV. Your three reviewer-facing comments go at the three places the worksheet marks. The comments the R Companion writes say what the code does. They do not count as your three, which name a decision and why.

**Length:** The worksheet's code, 50 to 150 lines with its comments, with each of the three reviewer-facing comments 40 to 100 words. Word counts cover your own writing, not the title, headings, tables, references, figure captions, code, or output, and writing more than the range never costs points.

**AI-use log:** submit the [AI-use log (.docx)](resources/AI-use-log.docx) with this assignment, with an entry for each time an AI tool shaped it, or with the no-AI box checked.

**Rubric:** [Data Wrangling in R rubric (PDF)](resources/rubrics/MC501-rubric-data-wrangling-in-r.pdf). It lists the nine requirements, including the three reviewer-facing comments, and the points for each.

**Worksheet:** [11-wrangling-data.qmd](starters/11-wrangling-data.qmd), the worksheet you fill in and submit.

**Risks guide:** [Data Wrangling risks guide](resources/risks/data-wrangling.qmd). The traps on this job, what each looks like, and how to check for it. It shows no answers.

**How-to:** [Wrangling](guides/mc501/08-wrangling.md) step-by-step guide, and the [Wrangling and the reliability grid](https://siue.yuja.com/V/Video?v=17490319&a=95173025) walkthrough video.

</details>

### Inferencing Data in R {#inferencing-data-in-r}

**100 points. Due Monday, December 7, 11:59 PM.** *(Week 15)*

Test four relationships, one per test, and report how big each is.

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>What to submit, and the rubric</summary>

**What you submit:** the filled worksheet and the HTML it renders to, uploaded to Blackboard under Inferencing Data in R. The worksheet is part 3 of the Twitch job: four hypotheses written before any code, then four tests, one of them on the thirty messages you hand-coded in Data Wrangling, each with its assumptions, effect size, and interval. Optional: the Test group of the R Companion's **Write R code** writes the four tests for your settings-block variables, the plain R call first and the `v2v` wrapper after it as a check, and its **APA numbers to check your sentence** prints a test's numbers in APA form. The hypotheses, the reason for each test, the four reports, and the interpretation are your own writing. Assumption checks are not generated; the Test group's **Power analysis for your sample size** writes the `pwr.t.test()` call for your design, and what its answer means for your study stays your own writing.

**Length:** 700 to 1,100 words of your own writing (hypotheses, justifications, diagnostics, the four reports and the two paragraphs), not counting code or output. Word counts cover your own writing, not the title, headings, tables, references, figure captions, code, or output, and writing more than the range never costs points.

**Part of the White Paper:** a draft of the Results section's tests, with the limits paragraph a draft of part of the Discussion. The paper reruns this script on your own variables; the Twitch numbers stay here.

**AI-use log:** submit the [AI-use log (.docx)](resources/AI-use-log.docx) with this assignment, with an entry for each time an AI tool shaped it, or with the no-AI box checked.

**Rubric:** [Inferencing Data in R rubric (PDF)](resources/rubrics/MC501-rubric-inferencing-data-in-r.pdf). It lists each step from the four hypotheses to what the results do not license, and the points for each.

**Worksheet:** [13-inferencing-data-mc501.qmd](starters/13-inferencing-data-mc501.qmd), the worksheet you fill in and submit.

**Risks guide:** [Inferencing Data risks guide](resources/risks/inferencing-data.qmd). The traps on this job, what each looks like, and how to check for it. It shows no answers.

**How-to:** [Tests](guides/mc501/10-tests-and-check-my-test-choice.md) step-by-step guide, and the [Tests](https://siue.yuja.com/V/Video?v=17490908&a=168993969) walkthrough video.

</details>

## Phase V: The Publisher {#phase-v-the-publisher}

*Inference and Publication.* Test the relationship and publish the result. [Phase page](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/modules/05_publisher/?edition=mc501)

### White Paper and conference poster {#white-paper-and-conference-poster}

**200 points. Due Friday, December 18, 11:59 PM.**

The final deliverable: your study written up in IMRaD, rendered to PDF, published to the web, and carried onto a conference poster.

**Dated step, Monday, December 7, 11:59 PM:** push the full coded dataset and a re-code of a fresh subsample to your project repository. The stability figure in Methods earns its points only if that commit is dated on or before December 7; the rubric carries the subsample rule. Nothing about your analysis is due that day.

<details class="syl-policy">
<summary>What to submit, and the rubric</summary>

**What you submit:** three things, all required: the paper as a PDF, the poster as a PDF, and the live URL of your GitHub Pages site. Upload both PDFs and paste the URL into the Blackboard submission for White Paper and conference poster; the submission is incomplete without each.

**Length:** The paper 5,000 to 7,000 words from the introduction through the reflection, plus the 150 to 250 word abstract; the poster one page of 400 to 800 words. Word counts cover your own writing, not the title, headings, tables, references, figure captions, code, or output, and writing more than the range never costs points.

**AI-use log:** submit the [AI-use log (.docx)](resources/AI-use-log.docx) with this assignment, with an entry for each time an AI tool shaped it, or with the no-AI box checked.

**Rubric:** [White Paper and conference poster rubric (PDF)](resources/rubrics/MC501-rubric-white-paper-and-conference-poster.pdf). It lists what each section of the paper carries, including the three transparency markers, what the poster shows, and the points for each.

</details>
